title: How should we change teaching and assessment in response to increasingly powerful generative Artificial Intelligence? Outcomes of the ChatGPT teacher survey
extended_summary:
This paper asks how educators believe teaching and assessment should change in response to the rapid emergence of generative AI such as ChatGPT, and what motivates those changes. The study frames generative AI as a disruptive educational technology and argues that teacher beliefs and motivations are important baseline evidence for understanding future adoption and pedagogical change.

The authors used a mixed-methods survey design with 318 educators from a diverse set of teaching levels, regions, experience levels, and discipline areas. Participants were recruited online through social media and professional teaching networks. The survey measured perceived impact of generative AI on teaching and assessment, as well as open-ended views on what should change in curriculum, pedagogy, and assessment, and why educators felt motivated to change.

Overall, most respondents expected ChatGPT-like tools to have a major or profound impact on teaching and assessment, though a substantial minority predicted little or no impact. Greater prior awareness of generative AI predicted higher perceived impact. Qualitative responses suggested that teachers wanted more emphasis on learning about AI, critical thinking, ethics, process-oriented and authentic tasks, face-to-face or supervised assessment, and using AI as an aid for lesson design and exemplars. The authors conclude that generative AI is likely to drive pedagogical and assessment redesign, but their findings reflect teacher perceptions rather than evidence that these changes are effective.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot and large language model system for natural-language text generation and interaction.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers were surveyed about how ChatGPT and similar generative AI tools might affect teaching and assessment, and about how they might use ChatGPT in curriculum, pedagogy, and assessment design.

findings.finding_summary: In this mixed-methods survey of educators (n=318), 93% of respondents said ChatGPT/generative AI would have at least a minor impact on teaching, with 73% rating the impact as major or profound and only 7% selecting none. Mean perceived impact on teaching was 2.7/4, and on assessment was 2.8/4; higher AI awareness predicted higher perceived impact.
findings.measure: Perceived impact of ChatGPT/generative AI on teaching and on assessment (4-point Likert scale: none to profound)
findings.effect_size: teaching: Cohen's d=0.45 for high vs low/medium awareness; assessment: Cohen's d=0.35 for high vs low/medium awareness

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported multiple intended changes to teaching in response to ChatGPT, including teaching students how AI works (n=40), critical thinking/evaluating AI responses (n=38), ethical and responsible use of AI (n=26), and using ChatGPT as exemplars/models (n=17). A subset reported no planned change to teaching (n=31), and only three respondents said they would discourage AI use.
findings.measure: Open-ended teacher-reported intended changes to teaching practice

findings.finding_summary: For assessment, teachers suggested changes such as spoken tasks (n=29), examinations (n=21), higher-order thinking tasks (n=71), authentic tasks (n=65), process-focused assessment (n=50), and more supervision/invigilated assessment (n=69). Some also proposed embedding AI into assessment tasks (n=54), while 36 respondents said ChatGPT would have minimal or no impact on assessment tasks.
findings.measure: Open-ended teacher-reported intended changes to assessment practice

quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional mixed-methods survey rather than an experimental or longitudinal study. It provides useful educator perceptions at scale, but it does not test actual repeated use, coaching outcomes, or causal effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports mostly perceived impact and intended practice changes, not measured student or teacher outcome effects. Findings suggest substantial anticipated influence of ChatGPT, but no direct evidence of harm, attrition, or sustained-use performance effects.
